title: Your own faults
hook: look not at others' faults but at what you have done and left undone (Dhammapada 50)
tomorrow: which knocks you over faster: praise or blame?

segments.voice: Yesterday, earnest: appamada, heedful care, the word in the Buddha's last sentence. Today, the verses turn the heedful eye around.

Some group chats have one: the person who screenshots everyone else's mistakes. The Dhammapada has a verse for that. Verse fifty, in plain words: don't look at the faults of others, at what they've done or left undone; look at what you yourself have done and left undone. Which leaves yesterday's question hanging: should you ever point out someone else's faults? Inside the Buddhist tradition, two answers live side by side, and both have a case.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SCREENSHOTS.` → `WHAT YOU'VE DONE AND LEFT UNDONE.` → `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH WITH A CASE.`

segments.voice: The first answer comes with a story. The commentary tells of a woman who fed a wandering ascetic named Pathika like her own son. When she invited the Buddha to her house, Pathika stood outside and cursed her. Shaken, she couldn't take in the teaching. The Buddha told her not to mind his words, and spoke verse fifty: watch your own deeds, what you've done and left undone. View one, then: other people's faults are a distraction, and your own list is the only one you can change. Now view two. At the end of the rains retreat, monks hold a ceremony called Pavarana, the invitation. Each monk asks the whole community: if you have seen, heard or suspected any fault in me, tell me, out of compassion, and I'll make it right. And in another sutta the Buddha gives five conditions for anyone who corrects another: speak at the right time, truly, gently, for their good, and with goodwill. View two's best case: a fault nobody names can't be mended, and kind correction is a gift. Notice what they share. In Pavarana, the one who asks is the one with faults. And the five conditions are a check the speaker runs on himself before he says a word. One way to hold both: your own list first, and correction only when it's timely and kind. The two views speak to different moments, and the tradition keeps both.
screen: `PATHIKA CURSES AT THE DOOR.` · `VIEW ONE: WATCH YOUR OWN DEEDS.` · `VIEW TWO: PAVARANA, THE INVITATION.` · `FIVE CONDITIONS FOR SPEAKING.` · then, large: `MY OWN LIST.`

segments.voice: Look at your own two hands for a moment: the hands that did today's things. Silently name one thing they did and one thing they left undone. No one else's name comes into it. Then rest the hands and sit with your own list, without fixing it.
Your own faults: what you've done and left undone. The Dhammapada's mirror, and Pavarana's invitation to hear about them.
The line for today: my own list, the only one I can change tonight. Three verses in, and that's the day.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, the Pavarana ceremony at the end of the rains retreat has each monk invite the community to point out any fault seen, heard or suspected; lay Buddhists often reflect on their own conduct as part of practice.
